## 1 Introduction

This micro case illustrates the risks associated with using multiple
instruments when some of them may be invalid. While adding instruments
can increase precision, invalid instruments can reintroduce bias into
IV estimators.

## 2 Data Generating Process

We simulate a setting with one valid instrument and one invalid instrument.
The invalid instrument directly affects the outcome, violating the
exclusion restriction.

```{r dgp}
set.seed(123)

n <- 3000

u <- rnorm(n)

# Instruments
z1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)  # valid
z2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)  # invalid

# Treatment assignment
treat <- 0.8 * z1 + 0.6 * u + rnorm(n)
treat <- as.integer(treat > median(treat))

# Potential outcomes
y0 <- 5 + u + 1.5 * z2 + rnorm(n)  # z2 violates exclusion
y1 <- y0 + 2

# Observed outcome
y <- y0 + treat * (y1 - y0)

case3D <- data.frame(y, treat, z1, z2, u, y0, y1)
```

## 3 OLS Benchmark

```{r ols}
ols <- lm(y ~ treat, data = case3D)
summary(ols)
```

## 4 IV with a Valid Instrument

Using only the valid instrument recovers the causal effect.

```{r iv-valid}
library(AER)
iv_valid <- ivreg(y ~ treat | z1, data = case3D)
summary(iv_valid)
```

## 5 IV with Multiple Instruments (One Invalid)

We now include both instruments, one of which violates the exclusion
restriction.

```{r iv-invalid}
iv_invalid <- ivreg(y ~ treat | z1 + z2, data = case3D)
summary(iv_invalid)
```

## 6 Overidentification Test

The Sargan test evaluates whether the instruments are jointly valid.
Rejection suggests at least one invalid instrument, but non-rejection
does not guarantee validity.

```{r sargan}
library(AER)
sargan(iv_invalid)
```

## 7 Interpretation

Adding invalid instruments can bias IV estimates, even when the model is
overidentified. Overidentification tests are useful diagnostics, but they
cannot confirm instrument validity.

## 8 Conclusion

This case demonstrates that more instruments are not necessarily better.
Instrument validity is more important than instrument quantity.
